lessons.title: Start here
lessons.summary: The workflow, files and scientific questions behind your first calculation.

blocks.html:
Learn to build SIESTA, run a two-atom silicon calculation, choose numerical settings, and check a relaxed structure. These lessons follow Charles Rotich's supplied files and results, with complete downloads so you can inspect every input.

Choose your starting point

If you are new to scientific computing, follow the lessons in order. If SIESTA already works on your machine, start with the silicon input and first SCF lesson. Experienced readers can open the convergence tables and reference outputs directly.

Lesson You will be able to
Installation Build an MPI-enabled executable with Ubuntu system libraries
Silicon input Explain the cell, basis, functional and numerical controls
First SCF Run a calculation and confirm electronic convergence
Convergence Compare mesh, k-point and lattice scans quantitatively
Relaxation Interpret force, stress and final-geometry checks
Troubleshooting Diagnose failures without confusing completion with convergence
Doxygen Document the teaching Python scripts and shell launcher

What you need

  • A Linux workstation or an allocated HPC compute node.
  • Bash and basic terminal navigation.
  • An MPI-enabled SIESTA build; the installation lesson targets Ubuntu 26.04.
  • Python 3 for the standard-library teaching scripts.
  • NumPy and Matplotlib only if you want to regenerate the original plots.

The installation lesson needs administrator access for Ubuntu packages. On a managed cluster, use the compiler/MPI modules approved by your administrators rather than installing workstation packages.

Download and inspect the course

Download the complete course ZIP from the Downloads page, extract it with your file manager, and open a terminal in the extracted computational-materials-learning folder.

blocks.code:
pwd
ls
ls examples/silicon-diamond

blocks.html:
You should see docs, examples, reference, scripts and doxygen. Run the lesson commands one block at a time; do not execute the Markdown file as a shell script.

The calculation workflow

  1. Define the material and physical model: silicon, PBEsol, a DZP basis, and a norm-conserving pseudopotential.
  2. Solve the electronic problem at fixed geometry: SCF.
  3. Check numerical accuracy by changing one setting at a time.
  4. Relax geometry using converged electronic calculations at each step.
  5. Inspect final forces, stress and structure; archive the inputs and output together.

SCF is the repeated solution of the electronic density and Hamiltonian until they agree within tolerance. Relaxation moves atoms or changes the cell using calculated forces and stress. A converged SCF cycle is necessary at each geometry, but does not by itself establish a converged geometry.

Where the evidence comes from

The course includes the author's completed runs and scan tables. The reference SCF reports -230.042602 eV for the two-atom primitive cell. The installation guide targets SIESTA 5.4.2, while the executable banner in both outputs reads unreleased e486d1206 (2025-12-16). Record that distinction when reproducing the work.

The reference files have been inspected. The SIESTA build and numerical calculations have not been repeated in the website-building environment. See the source audit for the exact provenance and limitations.

A small first exercise

Before running anything, answer: how many atoms are in the silicon input, and how many valence electrons should that pseudopotential provide? The input has two Si atoms; the PSML file specifies four valence electrons per Si, so the neutral cell contains eight.

Continue with installing SIESTA, or understanding the silicon input if your executable is already ready.

lessons.title: Install SIESTA
lessons.summary: Compilers, MPI, numerical libraries, configuration and build checkpoints.

headings.title: 3. Verify the compiler and MPI wrappers

blocks.html:
This lesson expands the author's Ubuntu 26.04 guide into a staged build with checkpoints. The main compiler, MPI and numerical libraries come from Ubuntu packages. SIESTA-specific dependencies such as libfdf or a compatible libgridxc may still be fetched and built by CMake; inspect the configure log to see what was actually used.

1. Check the environment

Use a normal Bash terminal. For this system-library route, deactivate Conda and avoid mixing private MPI or compiler paths with Ubuntu libraries. This lesson installs software on your existing Ubuntu system; it does not upgrade the operating system.

blocks.code:
cat /etc/os-release
command -v gcc gfortran cmake mpifort

blocks.html:
The reference output was produced on x86_64 with GNU 15.2.0. That is recorded provenance, not a requirement to copy a CPU-specific -march=native build onto other machines. Keep compiler and MPI versions consistent across the libraries you use.

2. Install the system packages

Refresh package information, then install the compiler/build tools and libraries used by this route:

blocks.code:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y \
  build-essential git wget curl cmake pkg-config \
  gcc g++ gfortran openmpi-bin libopenmpi-dev \
  libopenblas-dev liblapack-dev libscalapack-openmpi-dev \
  libfftw3-dev libfftw3-mpi-dev \
  libhdf5-openmpi-dev libnetcdf-dev libnetcdf-mpi-dev libnetcdff-dev \
  libxc-dev libxmlf90-dev libpsml-dev libxml2-dev \
  python3 python3-dev python3-venv \
  make ninja-build autoconf automake libtool m4 \
  bison flex texinfo unzip

blocks.html:
If a package has no installation candidate, stop and inspect apt-cache policy PACKAGE_NAME. Package availability depends on enabled Ubuntu repositories and architecture. Do not silently switch MPI implementations to get past a missing package.

Component Role
GCC / GFortran Compile C, C++ and Fortran code
CMake, Make / Ninja Configure and build the application
Open MPI Run and compile MPI parallel programs
OpenBLAS / LAPACK Dense linear algebra
ScaLAPACK Distributed linear algebra for MPI
FFTW FFT facilities where enabled
NetCDF / HDF5 Scientific I/O and post-processing support
LibXC / libgridxc Exchange-correlation functional support
libPSML / XMLF90 Read PSML pseudopotentials and XML

The teaching calculation uses ordinary diagonalisation. Native ELPA and ELSI are disabled in the configure command below to keep this first build smaller. This intentionally differs from the author's reference executable, which reports ELSI and external ELPA support. They can be introduced as an advanced build later.

3. Verify the compiler and MPI wrappers

blocks.code:
gcc --version | head -1
gfortran --version | head -1
cmake --version | head -1
command -v mpicc mpifort mpirun
mpifort --showme:command
mpifort --showme:link
pkg-config --modversion libxc xmlf90 libpsml

blocks.html:
The wrappers should identify the intended Ubuntu toolchain. A library version string is useful evidence; it is not proof that CMake selected that exact installation. The next log is the decisive check.

4. Prepare the source

Use dedicated versioned directories. These commands stop if a source folder already exists instead of deleting an existing installation.

blocks.code:
export SIESTA_SRC="$HOME/src/siesta-5.4.2"
export SIESTA_BUILD="$HOME/build/siesta-5.4.2-system"
export SIESTA_PREFIX="$HOME/local/siesta-5.4.2-system"
export NBUILD="$(nproc)"
mkdir -p "$HOME/src" "$HOME/build" "$HOME/local"
test ! -e "$SIESTA_SRC" || { echo 'Source directory exists; inspect or reuse it.'; false; }

blocks.html: If the last command fails, resolve the existing folder before continuing. Download the source only after that check passes:

blocks.code:
wget -O "$HOME/src/siesta-5.4.2.tar.gz" \
  https://gitlab.com/siesta-project/siesta/-/archive/5.4.2/siesta-5.4.2.tar.gz
tar -xzf "$HOME/src/siesta-5.4.2.tar.gz" -C "$HOME/src"
ls "$SIESTA_SRC"
mkdir -p "$SIESTA_BUILD"

blocks.html:
For a later session, re-export these four variables. Build directories are tied to the compiler and MPI used during configuration; use another dedicated build directory when changing toolchains.

5. Configure

Enable pipefail so a failed CMake command is not hidden by successful logging through tee.

blocks.code:
set -o pipefail
cmake \
  -S "$SIESTA_SRC" -B "$SIESTA_BUILD" \
  -G "Unix Makefiles" \
  -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX="$SIESTA_PREFIX" \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=mpicc \
  -DCMAKE_Fortran_COMPILER=mpifort \
  -DSIESTA_WITH_MPI=ON \
  -DSIESTA_WITH_OPENMP=OFF \
  -DSIESTA_WITH_NETCDF=ON \
  -DSIESTA_WITH_LIBXC=ON \
  -DSIESTA_WITH_FLOOK=OFF \
  -DSIESTA_WITH_ELPA=OFF \
  -DSIESTA_WITH_ELSI=OFF \
  -DBLAS_LIBRARY=openblas \
  -DLAPACK_LIBRARY=openblas \
  -DSCALAPACK_LIBRARY=-lscalapack-openmpi \
  2>&1 | tee "$SIESTA_BUILD/siesta-configure.log"

blocks.html: Library names avoid the original guide's hard-coded x86_64 library paths. If detection fails, use the actual paths reported by your package manager; keep the selected libraries consistent with Open MPI. Required domain-library compatibility may cause CMake to build a bundled dependency.

blocks.code:
tail -40 "$SIESTA_BUILD/siesta-configure.log"
grep -Ei 'MPI|BLAS|LAPACK|NETCDF|LIBXC|PSML|GRIDXC|FDF' \
  "$SIESTA_BUILD/CMakeCache.txt"

blocks.html:
Continue only after configuration and generation succeed. Review warnings about unused manually specified variables and missing libraries rather than treating a partially generated folder as a completed build.

6. Build, test and install

blocks.code:
cmake --build "$SIESTA_BUILD" --parallel "$NBUILD" \
  2>&1 | tee "$SIESTA_BUILD/siesta-build.log"
ctest --test-dir "$SIESTA_BUILD" --output-on-failure \
  2>&1 | tee "$SIESTA_BUILD/siesta-ctest.log"
cmake --install "$SIESTA_BUILD"

blocks.html:
On a low-memory machine, reduce NBUILD before building. Passing tests is useful only if tests were actually discovered and run; a "No tests were found" message is not equivalent to a validated scientific installation.

7. Activate and check

blocks.code:
export PATH="$SIESTA_PREFIX/bin:$PATH"
hash -r
command -v siesta
ldd "$SIESTA_PREFIX/bin/siesta" | grep -E 'mpi|blas|scalapack|netcdf|xc|not found'

blocks.html: not found indicates a missing shared library. On a dynamically linked build, confirm that the MPI library paths match the Ubuntu MPI wrappers used during configuration. To activate SIESTA in future terminals, add these lines once to ~/.bashrc using your editor:

blocks.code:
export SIESTA_HOME="$HOME/local/siesta-5.4.2-system"
export PATH="$SIESTA_HOME/bin:$PATH"

blocks.html:
Open a new terminal, or source your edited file. Your first completed SCF output will supply the executable banner and a small end-to-end numerical check.

Keep the build record

Retain configure, build and test logs, the compiler/MPI versions and the first successful output. The author's note names 5.4.2, but the supplied outputs display a commit banner. Record what your executable prints rather than promising identical results from every build.

Sources: author's original guide, official SIESTA build instructions, and Ubuntu package catalogue.

lessons.title: Understand the silicon input
lessons.summary: Explain the primitive cell, pseudopotential, basis and every important control.

headings.title: Why the lattice constant is half the cubic parameter

blocks.html:
This example is elemental silicon in the diamond structure. It uses a two-atom primitive cell. Carbon diamond and silicon carbide are different systems; neither is represented by this input.

The physical model

Setting Supplied value
Atoms / species 2 Si atoms / 1 species
Functional GGA PBEsol
Basis Split, double-zeta plus polarisation (DZP)
Pseudopotential Si PSML, norm-conserving, scalar relativistic
Valence electrons 4 per Si; 8 in the neutral cell
Real-space grid MeshCutoff 200 Ry
k-point mesh 10×10×10, no shift
Final DM tolerance 1.0d-7
Charge 0
Spin Non-polarised in the supplied output

The final inputs do not specify every basis-confinement setting, electronic temperature or solver default. For exact reproduction, retain the echoed input and reported settings from the output alongside the executable version.

Why the lattice constant is half the cubic parameter

The dimensionless primitive vectors are (0,1,1), (1,0,1) and (1,1,0). SIESTA multiplies them by LatticeConstant. For this representation, the conventional cubic parameter is a = 2 × LatticeConstant.

blocks.code:
LatticeConstant     2.72105 Ang

%block LatticeVectors
   0.0   1.0   1.0
   1.0   0.0   1.0
   1.0   1.0   0.0
%endblock LatticeVectors

blocks.html:
Thus a = 5.44210 Å; each primitive-vector length is about 3.848146 Å, and the primitive volume is about 40.293924 Å³. The two basis atoms sit at fractional coordinates (0,0,0) and (¼,¼,¼) relative to the primitive vectors. Do not interpret those coordinates as fractions of a conventional cubic cell.

Complete SCF input

Download si_scf.fdf. The supplied input is:

blocks.code:
SystemName          Si_PBEsol_LatticeScan
SystemLabel         Si
NumberOfAtoms       2
NumberOfSpecies     1

%block ChemicalSpeciesLabel
   1   14   Si
%endblock ChemicalSpeciesLabel

PAO.BasisType       split
PAO.BasisSize       DZP
XC.functional       GGA
XC.authors          PBEsol

LatticeConstant     2.72105 Ang
%block LatticeVectors
   0.0   1.0   1.0
   1.0   0.0   1.0
   1.0   1.0   0.0
%endblock LatticeVectors

AtomicCoordinatesFormat Fractional
%block AtomicCoordinatesAndAtomicSpecies
   0.000000   0.000000   0.000000   1
   0.250000   0.250000   0.250000   1
%endblock AtomicCoordinatesAndAtomicSpecies

MeshCutoff          200 Ry
%block kgrid.MonkhorstPack
   10   0    0    0.0
    0  10    0    0.0
    0   0   10    0.0
%endblock kgrid.MonkhorstPack

MaxSCFIterations    150
DM.Tolerance        1.0d-7
DM.MixingWeight     0.10
SolutionMethod      diagon
NetCharge           0.0

blocks.html:
The historical SystemName contains "LatticeScan" even though this file runs one SCF calculation. The run type is determined by the input options, not by this descriptive name.

Read the important controls

Entry Meaning What changes if you edit it?
SystemLabel Prefix for SIESTA-generated files Output names and restart-file names
ChemicalSpeciesLabel Species index, atomic number and symbol Species-to-pseudopotential mapping
PAO.BasisSize Local orbital basis size Variational flexibility, cost and basis error
XC.authors Exchange-correlation choice Physical approximation; match the pseudopotential
MeshCutoff Real-space integration-grid fineness Grid accuracy and cost; not a plane-wave basis cutoff
kgrid.MonkhorstPack Reciprocal-space sampling Brillouin-zone integration accuracy
DM.Tolerance Density-matrix convergence threshold Electronic stopping accuracy
DM.MixingWeight Mixing weight used during SCF Convergence behaviour; not an accuracy guarantee
MaxSCFIterations Upper limit on SCF cycles Allows more attempts; does not guarantee convergence
SolutionMethod Electronic solver diagon uses diagonalisation
NetCharge Cell charge relative to neutrality Electron count and charged-system treatment

SIESTA 5.4 normally mixes the Hamiltonian; a DM.* option name alone does not establish that density-matrix mixing was selected. The reference output explicitly reports Hamiltonian mixing and a DM+H convergence criterion.

Check the pseudopotential

Use the supplied Si.psml rather than substituting a similarly named file. The author attributes it to PseudoDojo, PBEsol, scalar-relativistic NC, stringent, PSML.

blocks.code: sha256sum examples/silicon-diamond/pseudopotentials/Si.psml

blocks.html: Expected SHA-256:

blocks.code: fa0e9fa6ca7a97ab07879cd1bc8d858ebb32a90f262535b578d14d4d515bdc95

blocks.html:
Its embedded provenance identifies ONCVPSP 3.3.0, PSML 1.1, LibXC PBEsol IDs 116 and 133, and four valence electrons. The author's collection label v0.4.1 is preserved separately in the source audit.

Exercise: if LatticeConstant were changed to 5.44210 Ang while keeping these dimensionless vectors, the intended cubic parameter would double. This is why cell conventions must be stated explicitly.

Continue to your first SCF run. Parameter reference: SIESTA 5.4 manual.

lessons.title: Run your first SCF calculation
lessons.summary: Launch a fresh run, check convergence and read the supplied reference result.

blocks.html:
At fixed atomic positions and cell vectors, solve the electronic problem until the density matrix and Hamiltonian satisfy the chosen tolerances. This lesson uses the input from the previous page and the same PBEsol Si pseudopotential.

1. Prepare a fresh directory

Start in the extracted course folder:

blocks.code:
mkdir -p runs
export SCF_RUN="$(mktemp -d "$PWD/runs/scf-manual-XXXXXX")"
cp examples/silicon-diamond/scf/si_scf.fdf "$SCF_RUN/si.fdf"
cp examples/silicon-diamond/pseudopotentials/Si.psml "$SCF_RUN/"
cd "$SCF_RUN"
ls

blocks.html:
You should see si.fdf and Si.psml. A fresh folder makes the initial condition clear and avoids an accidental density-matrix restart from an unrelated calculation.

2. Run one of these alternatives

For a small one-process run:

blocks.code:
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=1
export OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1
siesta < si.fdf > si.out 2> si.err

blocks.html: For an MPI-enabled executable with four processes:

blocks.code:
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=1
export OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1
mpirun -np 4 siesta < si.fdf > si.out 2> si.err

blocks.html:
Choose a process count supported by your machine or allocation. Four processes is the supplied script's example; it is not a universal optimum. A two-atom calculation may be faster with fewer processes because MPI has overhead.

The < operator supplies the input; > writes standard output; 2> captures standard error. On a cluster, put the launch inside an allocation using the scheduler's recommended launcher. The archive does not contain a verified Slurm submission script.

3. Inspect progress and completion

blocks.code:
tail -30 si.out
grep -E 'SCF cycle converged|Job completed' si.out
grep 'siesta:         Total =' si.out | tail -1
grep 'siesta:         Fermi =' si.out | tail -1

blocks.html:
Check both electronic convergence and normal termination. A finite energy printed during an incomplete job does not establish success.

The supplied SCF reference output reports:

blocks.code:
SCF cycle converged after 18 iterations
siesta:         Total =    -230.042602
siesta:         Fermi =      -4.326879
Job completed

blocks.html:
4. Interpret the result

Quantity Reference Interpretation
Total energy -230.042602 eV Energy of the two-atom computational cell
Fermi energy -4.326879 eV Fermi level in this calculation's internal potential convention
SCF cycles 18 Electronic iterations in the supplied run
Electrons 8 Neutral cell with four valence electrons per Si

Absolute total energy depends on the pseudopotential, basis and numerical choices. It is useful for comparing compatible calculations of the same system; it is not by itself a formation energy or cohesive energy. The reported Fermi level is not vacuum-aligned, and does not give the band gap by itself.

Small differences across machines and builds are possible. If the difference is substantial, compare the echoed input, pseudopotential hash, basis defaults, mesh, k-grid, solver and convergence criteria before drawing a physical conclusion.

5. Use the portable launcher

Return to the course root. The supplied teaching helper performs the fresh-folder setup and validation for you:

blocks.code: bash scripts/run_calculation.sh scf 4

blocks.html: It prints a new runs/scf-... path and a JSON summary. Inspect the output directly as well. You can independently read the author's output without running SIESTA:

blocks.code: python3 scripts/read_results.py reference/silicon-diamond/scf_si/si_scf.out

blocks.html:
The output reader checks final energy, an SCF-convergence message and normal completion. Geometry convergence and numerical convergence are separate checks.

Check your understanding

If the SCF cycle reaches its maximum iteration count, adding more iterations may help, but the reason could be unstable mixing or an unsuitable setup. Examine the convergence history before changing several settings at once.

Continue to convergence tests. Keep si.fdf, Si.psml, si.out, si.err and the executable banner together as your run record.

lessons.title: Test numerical convergence
lessons.summary: Compare mesh, k-point and lattice scans using the author's actual data.

headings.title: Mesh, k-points and basis are different checks

blocks.html:
Change one numerical setting at a time while keeping the physical system fixed. The archive contains three scan tables and their original figures: mesh cutoff, k-point sampling and the conventional lattice parameter.

Mesh, k-points and basis are different checks

MeshCutoff controls the real-space integration grid. The k-grid samples reciprocal space. The DZP basis describes the orbitals. Converging one does not converge the other two.

The supplied mesh scan fixes the k-grid at 10×10×10 and the cubic lattice parameter at 5.44 Å. The supplied k-point scan uses 400 Ry. Both use DM.Tolerance 1.0d-5; the final SCF and relaxation inputs tighten this to 1.0d-7.

1. Compare the mesh-cutoff scan

Use the highest sampled cutoff, 500 Ry, as the comparison reference. Define ΔE = E(setting) − E(reference). The sign is retained; for a tolerance use its absolute value.

MeshCutoff (Ry) Energy (eV / two-atom cell) ΔE versus 500 Ry (meV / cell)
100 -230.042930 -0.342
150 -230.042466 +0.122
200 -230.042593 -0.005
250 -230.042593 -0.005
300 -230.042571 +0.017
350 -230.042571 +0.017
400 -230.042616 -0.028
450 -230.042588 0.000
500 -230.042588 0.000

The author selected 200 Ry. It differs from the 500 Ry value by 0.005 meV per cell in this table, and subsequent mesh settings fluctuate slightly. This is an energy check for this fixed geometry. It does not demonstrate force or stress convergence for an arbitrary system, and does not justify a universal 200 Ry recommendation.

Real-space grid integration need not yield a strictly monotonic energy curve. Do not choose the most negative point automatically. For accurate relaxation, repeat convergence checks for forces and stress as well.

2. Compare the k-point scan

Use 14×14×14 as the highest sampled reference. Two atoms per cell means a meV/cell difference is divided by two to get meV/atom.

k-grid Energy (eV / cell) ΔE (meV / cell) ΔE (meV / atom)
2×2×2 -227.409044 2634.338 1317.169
4×4×4 -229.848165 195.217 97.6085
6×6×6 -230.018149 25.233 12.6165
8×8×8 -230.039232 4.150 2.075
10×10×10 -230.042616 0.766 0.383
12×12×12 -230.043250 0.132 0.066
14×14×14 -230.043382 0.000 0.000

A 10×10×10 mesh passes an illustrative 1 meV/atom energy threshold against the largest sampled mesh. That threshold is a teaching choice, not a stated experimental error bar or proof that band edges, optical properties and stress are equally converged.

3. Find the lattice minimum

The lattice scan fixes the 10×10×10 grid and 200 Ry cutoff. Each point is an SCF calculation at a different cell size. There is no cell relaxation within each point.

Cubic a (Å) LatticeConstant (Å) Energy (eV / cell)
5.36 2.68 -230.017451
5.38 2.69 -230.028411
5.40 2.70 -230.036189
5.42 2.71 -230.040895
5.44 2.72 -230.042593
5.46 2.73 -230.041379
5.48 2.74 -230.037436
5.50 2.75 -230.030805
5.52 2.76 -230.021541

The original plotting script fits the five points from 5.40 through 5.48 Å to E(a) = A a² + B a + C. Its minimum is a₀ = −B / (2A). Re-evaluating that fit from the supplied table gives 5.44206294 Å, or LatticeConstant = 2.72103147 Å. The final supplied input uses 2.72105 Å, a nearby rounded choice.

This is a local quadratic interpolation, not a full equation-of-state analysis. The original plot extends the local polynomial over the entire shown range; avoid interpreting that extrapolation as additional calculated points.

4. Re-run the scans

From the course root:

blocks.code:
python3 scripts/run_convergence.py mesh --np 4
python3 scripts/run_convergence.py kpoints --np 4
python3 scripts/run_convergence.py lattice --np 4

blocks.html:
These helpers retain the original template settings, create a fresh directory for each scan and write results.dat after each completed point. They stop if MPI fails or the output lacks electronic convergence, normal completion or final energy.

For a tighter study, copy a template, change its DM tolerance deliberately and label the new results accordingly. Do not replace the reference tables with newly generated values from a different setup without recording that change.

5. Rebuild the supplied plots

If NumPy and Matplotlib are not available, create a small analysis environment:

blocks.code:
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install numpy matplotlib

blocks.html: Then, for example:

blocks.code:
cd reference/silicon-diamond/convergence/lattice
python3 plot_lattice.py

blocks.html:
Each original plotting script reads its adjacent .dat file and writes a PNG. In a headless terminal use MPLBACKEND=Agg python3 plot_lattice.py. These plotting scripts analyse existing data; they do not run SIESTA.

What still needs testing

There is no supplied SZ/DZP/TZP comparison or basis-confinement scan. For a research-quality accuracy assessment, converge the observable you will report: lattice parameters, forces, stress, band edges or energy differences. A small absolute energy change alone is not a complete uncertainty budget.

Continue to relaxing the structure.

lessons.title: Relax the silicon structure
lessons.summary: Understand atomic and cell relaxation, force tolerances and stress checks.

headings.title: 3. Inspect forces, stress and final structure
4. Why the cell did not visibly move

blocks.html:
Use converged electronic calculations to compute forces and stress, then allow the optimisation algorithm to change atomic positions and the cell. The supplied example uses conjugate gradients (CG) with variable-cell relaxation.

1. Add the relaxation controls

The complete si_relax.fdf contains the SCF model from the earlier lesson plus these controls:

blocks.code:
MD.TypeOfRun        CG
MD.Steps            200
MD.VariableCell     .true.
MD.MaxForceTol      0.01 eV/Ang
MD.MaxStressTol     0.1 GPa
MD.TargetPressure   0.0 GPa

blocks.html:
Entry What it controls
MD.TypeOfRun CG Conjugate-gradient geometry minimisation
MD.Steps 200 Maximum optimisation steps, not a requirement to take 200 steps
MD.VariableCell true Optimise cell vectors as well as atomic positions
MD.MaxForceTol Required force threshold for the geometry
MD.MaxStressTol Required stress tolerance relative to the target
MD.TargetPressure Desired hydrostatic pressure

MD.Steps is the documented SIESTA 5.4 option; MD.NumCGsteps remains as a legacy option. For a fixed-cell atomic relaxation, set MD.VariableCell .false. in a separate input. Perfect bulk silicon has symmetry-constrained zero or near-zero forces, so fixed-cell relaxation alone cannot determine its equilibrium lattice parameter.

2. Launch in a new folder

From the course root:

blocks.code: bash scripts/run_calculation.sh relaxation 4

blocks.html:
The helper copies the input and matching pseudopotential into a fresh runs/relaxation-... directory. Its SCF-checking summary is useful, but it does not replace the geometry checks below.

The reference relaxation uses the same 200 Ry grid, 10×10×10 k-mesh and DM.Tolerance 1.0d-7 as the final SCF. It reports two electronic iterations. That shorter cycle can depend on the starting electronic state; it is not evidence that every fresh relaxation will converge in two iterations.

3. Inspect forces, stress and final structure

In your run directory:

blocks.code:
grep -E 'SCF cycle converged|cgvc:|Job completed' si.out
grep -A 10 'Atomic forces' si.out | tail -12
grep 'Stress tensor Voigt' si.out | tail -1
grep -A 3 'Relaxed atomic coordinates' si.out | tail -4
grep -A 4 'outcell: Unit cell vectors' si.out | tail -5

blocks.html:
The full reference relaxation output reports:

Quantity Reference Check
Maximum force 0.000011 eV/Å Below 0.01 eV/Å
Pressure -0.26020609 kbar Magnitude about 0.0260 GPa
Diagonal stress components About 0.26 kbar About 0.026 GPa, below the 0.1 GPa target tolerance
Final energy -230.042602 eV/cell Same printed value as the supplied SCF
Final volume 40.293924 Å³ Primitive two-atom cell

Remember 1 kbar = 0.1 GPa. Check the complete stress tensor, including shear components, rather than relying on hydrostatic pressure alone. A normal Job completed message can occur when the step limit is reached; compare the final diagnostics to the requested tolerances.

4. Why the cell did not visibly move

The starting cubic parameter is 5.44210 Å, already close to the fitted scan minimum of 5.44206294 Å. The reported forces and stress are below the chosen thresholds. The final vectors and fractional coordinates are unchanged at the printed precision:

This is a near-equilibrium convergence example. It does not demonstrate a large structural change or many geometry steps.

For a follow-up exercise, copy the input into a new directory and start at cubic a = 5.50 Å, which means LatticeConstant 2.75 Ang for these vectors. Run a fresh variable-cell relaxation and compare the final cell. That altered-start calculation has not been supplied or run here; label its results as your own new exercise.

5. Reuse the final geometry

SIESTA can write geometry/restart files during a calculation. Inspect the files your build actually produced. If an output geometry file is absent, the final outcell and outcoor blocks provide the reported geometry.

When transferring cell vectors already expressed in Å into an FDF block, use LatticeConstant 1.0 Ang with those physical vectors. Alternatively, keep the dimensionless primitive vectors and their scaling constant. Mixing both conventions would rescale the cell twice.

Read further

Official structural-optimisation tutorial and SIESTA 5.4 parameter reference.

Continue to troubleshooting and reproducibility.

lessons.title: Troubleshoot and reproduce
lessons.summary: Diagnose common failures and keep a complete calculation record.

headings.title: The relaxation finishes but the structure is wrong
What is and is not established here

blocks.html:
Start with the last successful stage: build, launch, pseudopotential reading, electronic convergence, or geometry convergence. Change one cause at a time and keep the failed output for comparison.

Installation and launch checks

Symptom Inspect first Next action
siesta: command not found command -v siesta and PATH Activate the installed bin directory
Shared library not found ldd output Resolve the missing library in the intended toolchain
MPI symbols / library conflicts MPI wrappers and CMakeCache Reconfigure in a dedicated build folder with one MPI stack
CMake cannot find a dependency Configure log and pkg-config metadata Check package installation and compatible paths
Process count rejected Available cores / scheduler allocation Reduce MPI count to fit the resources
Run ends without Job completed si.err and final output lines Diagnose the actual failure before accepting an energy

The installation guide uses pipefail with tee so build failures remain failures. Keep configure, build and test logs; the absence of the word "error" in a search is not enough to certify a successful build.

Missing or incorrect pseudopotential

The species label is Si, so this course places Si.psml beside the input. Verify the file exists and its hash matches the reference.

blocks.code:
ls -l Si.psml
sha256sum Si.psml

blocks.html:
A file with the correct name but a different functional, valence configuration or generation choice is a different scientific model. Do not compare its absolute energy directly against the reference without recording the change.

SCF does not converge

Inspect the iteration history, electronic occupations, initial geometry and mixed quantity. Lowering the mixing weight or allowing more iterations may help, but do not change the functional, basis, mesh and k-grid simultaneously just to make the message disappear.

SIESTA 5.4 normally mixes the Hamiltonian, even though several historical options have DM. names. Read the reported convergence criterion and mixed quantity in the output.

The relaxation finishes but the structure is wrong

Check the cell convention first. In this example, LatticeConstant is half the conventional cubic parameter. A scale-factor mistake can change the cell dramatically while the input remains syntactically valid.

Then inspect:

  • Final forces against the specified force tolerance.
  • All stress components against the target stress and tolerance.
  • Whether the maximum number of geometry steps was reached.
  • Whether cell relaxation was actually enabled.
  • Whether the intended cell/atomic constraints were used.

The author's starting geometry is already near equilibrium. An unchanged final structure is consistent with the small reported forces and stress.

Restart deliberately

DM.UseSaveDM can allow reading a saved density matrix. The teaching launchers use a fresh folder, making accidental reuse less likely. For an intentional restart, use compatible geometry/species/settings and keep the earlier input and output. Record that a restart was used.

Restart files are practical aids, not part of the small public reference package. Retain large files locally only when needed for continuation or analysis.

Reproducibility checklist

For each new run, save:

  1. The exact .fdf input and included files.
  2. The pseudopotential, upstream source and SHA-256 hash.
  3. SIESTA banner, source commit if known, compiler and MPI versions.
  4. Basis details, grid, k-mesh, electronic tolerance and spin/charge settings.
  5. Launch command, process count and any restart information.
  6. Complete output, error log and final structure.
  7. Analysis script and units used in each reported table.

What is and is not established here

The completed outputs and scan tables establish the reported example results. They do not supply basis-size convergence, a force/stress convergence study, raw per-point scan outputs, or proof that the reduced teaching build is identical to the reference executable. These gaps are recorded, not filled with guessed results.

If requesting help, provide the input, the first part of the output showing the build identity, the last output lines and the actual error. Share enough context to diagnose the stage that failed.

Continue to the Doxygen exercise. Full provenance: source audit.

lessons.title: Document the scripts with Doxygen
lessons.summary: Install Doxygen, read the supplied configuration and document your first Python utility.

headings.title: 6. Connect it to the learning website

blocks.html:
Doxygen can turn documented Python, C++, Fortran and Markdown into navigable HTML reference pages. This first exercise documents the teaching output reader and convergence launcher. It complements the learning pages by explaining how the utilities work.

1. Install and verify

On your Ubuntu computer:

blocks.code:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y doxygen graphviz
doxygen --version
dot -V

blocks.html:
Graphviz provides dot for supported diagrams. It does not create a scientifically meaningful workflow graph automatically from arbitrary shell commands.

2. Inspect the documented Python function

Open scripts/read_results.py. Its comments use the Doxygen-aware Python docstring form:

The code does not change when explanatory comments are added. Describe the function's actual behaviour, inputs, output units and failure conditions. Avoid documenting an assumed capability the script does not implement.

3. Use the supplied configuration

From the extracted course root:

blocks.code: doxygen doxygen/Doxyfile

blocks.html:
The prepared configuration points to the Python scripts, a code overview and the shell-usage page. It writes HTML to doxygen-output/html/ and does not generate LaTeX output.

Doxyfile setting Purpose
INPUT Files to document
USE_MDFILE_AS_MAINPAGE Use the code overview as the landing page
SOURCE_BROWSER Link to source listings
GENERATE_HTML Produce the HTML reference
OUTPUT_DIRECTORY Keep generated files in a separate folder
EXAMPLE_PATH Find the shell launcher used as an example
HAVE_DOT Allow supported Graphviz diagrams

To explore a fresh default configuration in a separate folder, doxygen -g Doxyfile generates one. The supplied short configuration is easier to review for this first exercise.

4. Open and inspect the result

blocks.code: xdg-open doxygen-output/html/index.html

blocks.html:
You should find the main page, file listings, Python function descriptions and a shell-launcher usage page. Inspect warnings: broken links, missing files or comments attached to the wrong function need correction before publication.

5. Understand the shell-script limit

Doxygen does not include a native Bash parser among its supported source-language parsers. The course therefore documents the shell launcher using doxygen/shell-usage.dox, with a usage explanation and included source listing. That provides useful readable reference without claiming automatic Bash call graphs.

Python function documentation can be generated directly. More advanced Python analysis and shell-specific documentation tooling can be evaluated later if the script collection grows.

6. Connect it to the learning website

Keep Markdown tutorials and original source code as the editable material. Regenerate Doxygen HTML when documented code changes, then publish the generated reference together with the course or under a dedicated code-reference path.

The current draft includes the configuration and a guided exercise. Doxygen HTML has not been generated in this environment, where the Doxygen executable is unavailable. Once you run the commands above and provide the generated output or warnings, we can inspect it and connect the verified HTML reference.

Official reading: Doxygen getting started, Python documentation comments, configuration reference, and Markdown support.
